title: Tenses
subject: english_grammar
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 English Language and Literature (184) syllabus, Section B Grammar: tenses, tested through gap filling, editing and transformation.

blocks.title: One verb, many times
blocks.body:
Read these three sentences:

- *Riya **plays** the sitar.*
- *Riya **is playing** the sitar.*
- *Riya **has played** the sitar.*

The same verb tells three different stories. The first says it is her habit, the second says it is happening right now, and the third says it is done and the result is with us. That small change in the verb is called **tense**, and it is the single most tested grammar topic in the CBSE board paper. Gap filling, editing and reported speech all depend on it.

In this chapter you will learn all twelve tenses through one simple map, the signal words that give the answer away, and the traps examiners set again and again.

blocks.title: Writing that anyone can read
blocks.body:
Ruskin Bond has written more than 500 stories, essays and novels from his home in the hills of Mussoorie. His sentences are short and clear, and his verbs always tell you exactly *when* something happens: a boy **was walking** through the forest, the rain **had stopped**, the leopard **will come back** tonight.

He was awarded the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1992 and the Padma Bhushan in 2014. His secret is not difficult words; it is correct, simple grammar used with care.
blocks.future: Strong English grammar opens doors to journalism, law, teaching, content writing, civil services, international business and every competitive exam.

blocks.question: Which sentence means that the keys are still missing now?
blocks.explanation: *Have lost* (present perfect) connects a past action to the present: the keys are still lost. *Lost yesterday* only tells us about the past; they may have been found.

blocks.title: Time and aspect
blocks.body:
Every tense answers two questions:

1. **When?** Present, past or future: this is the **time**.
2. **How?** This is the **aspect**:
   - **Simple:** the plain fact or habit.
   - **Continuous (progressive):** in progress, unfinished: *be* + V-ing.
   - **Perfect:** completed before a point of time: *have* + V3.
   - **Perfect continuous:** started earlier and still going on, or just stopped: *have been* + V-ing.

3 times × 4 aspects = **12 tenses**. Learn the helping verbs in the map below, and every tense becomes a simple formula.

**Verb forms:** V1 = base (*go*), V2 = past (*went*), V3 = past participle (*gone*), V-ing = present participle (*going*).

blocks.title: The twelve tenses
blocks.body:
| Time ↓ / Aspect → | Simple | Continuous | Perfect | Perfect continuous |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Present** | V1 / V1+s: *She writes.* | am/is/are + V-ing: *She is writing.* | has/have + V3: *She has written.* | has/have been + V-ing: *She has been writing.* |
| **Past** | V2: *She wrote.* | was/were + V-ing: *She was writing.* | had + V3: *She had written.* | had been + V-ing: *She had been writing.* |
| **Future** | will + V1: *She will write.* | will be + V-ing: *She will be writing.* | will have + V3: *She will have written.* | will have been + V-ing: *She will have been writing.* |

blocks.question: Which tense is used in: *They had been waiting for an hour.*?
blocks.explanation: *had been* + V-ing = past perfect continuous: the waiting went on for a time before a past moment.
option_feedback: That would be *were waiting*, without *had been*.
Correct!
Past perfect is *had* + V3 (*had waited*); here we have *had been* + V-ing.
That would be *have been waiting*; *had* shows the past.

blocks.title: Four ways to talk about now
blocks.body:
**1. Simple present (V1 / V1+s or es)**
- Habits and routines: *She **reads** the newspaper every morning.*
- Universal truths: *Water **boils** at 100 °C.* *The sun **rises** in the east.*
- Timetables and fixed schedules: *The train **leaves** at 6 p.m. tomorrow.*
- Headlines, quotations and commentary: *Kohli **hits** a six!*
- Rule: add **-s/-es** with *he, she, it* and singular nouns: *he goes, she watches, it flies*. Negatives and questions use *do/does* + V1: *She **does not like** tea.* (never *does not likes*)

**2. Present continuous (am/is/are + V-ing)**
- Action happening now: *The children **are playing** outside.*
- Temporary situations: *I **am staying** with my uncle this month.*
- Fixed future plans: *We **are meeting** the principal tomorrow.*

**3. Present perfect (has/have + V3)**
- Past action with a result now: *She **has broken** her arm.* (it is still broken)
- Experience up to now: *Have you ever **seen** snow?*
- With *just, already, yet, ever, never, so far, recently, since, for*.
- ✗ Never with a finished time: *I have seen him **yesterday*** is wrong. Say *I **saw** him yesterday.*

**4. Present perfect continuous (has/have been + V-ing)**
- Action that began in the past and is still going on: *He **has been studying** since 7 o'clock.* *They **have been living** here for ten years.*

**Stative verbs** (feelings, thoughts, senses, possession: *know, believe, like, love, want, belong, own, seem, understand*) are not normally used in the continuous: *I **know** the answer*, not *I am knowing the answer*.

blocks.title: Since or for?
blocks.body:
| **since** + a point of time | **for** + a length of time |
|---|---|
| since Monday, since 2019, since morning, since I was a child | for two hours, for three days, for a long time, for ages |
| *She has worked here **since 2019**.* | *She has worked here **for six years**.* |

blocks.question: Fill in the blank: My grandmother ____ yoga every morning for the last twenty years.
blocks.explanation: *for the last twenty years* + an action still going on = present perfect continuous: *has been doing*.
option_feedback: Correct!
*is doing* tells only about now; *for the last twenty years* needs an action that started long ago and still continues.
The simple present gives the habit, but *for the last twenty years* asks for the perfect continuous.
*did* puts the action fully in the past; she still does yoga.

blocks.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have finish the project last night.
I had finishing the project last night.
I finished the project last night.
I have finished the project last night.
blocks.explanation: A definite past time (*last night, yesterday, ago*) always takes the simple past.
option_feedback: After *have* we need V3 (*finished*), and *last night* still needs the simple past.
*had* is never followed by V-ing; and one past action does not need the past perfect.
Correct!
*last night* is a finished time, so the present perfect cannot be used.

blocks.title: Telling a story in the past
blocks.body:
**1. Simple past (V2)**
- A completed action at a definite time: *Gandhiji **returned** to India in 1915.*
- A series of actions in a story: *He **opened** the door, **looked** around and **left**.*
- Negatives and questions use *did* + **V1**: *He **did not go**.* *Did she **call**?* (✗ *did not went*, ✗ *did she called*)

**2. Past continuous (was/were + V-ing)**
- An action in progress at a past moment: *At 8 p.m. we **were having** dinner.*
- A longer action interrupted by a shorter one: *I **was crossing** the road **when** I **saw** the accident.* (long action = past continuous; short action = simple past)
- Two actions going on together: ***While** mother **was cooking**, father **was reading**.*

**3. Past perfect (had + V3)**: the *earlier* of two past actions.
- *The patient **had died** before the doctor **arrived**.* (first died, then arrived)
- *When we reached the station, the train **had** already **left**.*
- Only use it when there are two past actions and you need to show which came first.

**4. Past perfect continuous (had been + V-ing)**: an action that went on for some time before another past action.
- *She **had been waiting** for two hours when the bus finally **came**.*

blocks.title: Which happened first?
blocks.body:
| Sentence | First action (earlier) | Second action (later) |
|---|---|---|
| *The match **had started** when we **reached** the stadium.* | match started (past perfect) | we reached (simple past) |
| *After he **had finished** his work, he **went** home.* | finished work | went home |
| *I **was sleeping** when the phone **rang**.* | sleeping (going on) | phone rang (interrupted) |

blocks.question: Fill in the blank: When the firemen arrived, the house ____ to ashes.
blocks.explanation: The burning was completed before the firemen arrived: the earlier past action takes the past perfect, *had burnt*.
option_feedback: Both actions would then seem to happen together; the burning finished *before* the firemen came, so use the past perfect.
*has burnt* is present perfect; the story is in the past.
This means it was still burning; *to ashes* shows it was already completely burnt.
Correct!

blocks.question: Fill in the blank: She ____ a novel when the guests knocked at the door.
blocks.explanation: A longer action in progress (*was reading*) is interrupted by a short one (*knocked*).
option_feedback: The knock is in the past (*knocked*), so the reading must be in the past too.
Correct!
The reading was going on and was interrupted, so it needs the continuous: *was reading*.
*had read* means she had finished before they knocked; *when ... knocked* shows an interrupted action.

blocks.title: Will, going to and more
blocks.body:
English has no single future tense; it has several ways to talk about the future.

- **will + V1**: decisions made now, predictions, promises: *I **will help** you with the bags.* *It **will rain** tonight, I think.*
- **be going to + V1**: plans already made, and predictions from present evidence: *We **are going to buy** a car.* *Look at those clouds! It **is going to rain**.*
- **Present continuous**: fixed arrangements: *I **am flying** to Mumbai on Friday.*
- **Simple present**: timetables: *The exam **begins** on 15 February.*
- **Future continuous (will be + V-ing)**: in progress at a future time: *This time tomorrow I **will be travelling** to Shimla.*
- **Future perfect (will have + V3)**: completed before a future time: *By next March we **will have finished** the syllabus.*
- **Future perfect continuous (will have been + V-ing)**: duration up to a future time: *By June she **will have been teaching** for 25 years.*

**Golden rule for time clauses:** after *when, as soon as, before, after, until, if, unless*, use the **present**, not *will*:
*I will call you **when I reach** home.* (✗ *when I will reach*) *If it **rains**, the match will be cancelled.* (✗ *If it will rain*)

blocks.question: Fill in the blank: I will give him your message as soon as he ____.
blocks.explanation: Time clauses (*as soon as, when, before, until, if*) take the simple present even when the meaning is future.
option_feedback: The main clause is in the future (*will give*), so the time clause takes the simple present.
Arriving is a single short action, not one that continues.
Correct!
After *as soon as* (a time clause) we use the present, not *will*.

blocks.question: Fill in the blank: By the time you get there, the meeting ____.
blocks.explanation: *By the time* + a future moment → future perfect: completed before that moment.
option_feedback: Correct!
*will end* does not show that the ending happens *before* you get there.
*By the time you get there* is in the future; *ended* is past.
Present perfect cannot point to a future time.

sections.title: Board skills: signal words, sequence of tenses and traps

blocks.title: Signal words give the answer away
blocks.body:
| Signal words | Usual tense | Example |
|---|---|---|
| always, usually, often, every day, never (habit) | simple present | *He **walks** to school every day.* |
| now, at present, at the moment, Look!, Listen! | present continuous | *Look! The baby **is sleeping**.* |
| just, already, yet, ever, so far, recently, since, for (up to now) | present perfect | *I **have** just **finished** my homework.* |
| since / for + an action still going on | present perfect continuous | *It **has been raining** since morning.* |
| yesterday, last week, ago, in 2015, when (finished time) | simple past | *We **visited** Delhi two years ago.* |
| while, when (something interrupted) | past continuous | *I **was reading** when the lights went out.* |
| before, after, by the time, already (earlier past) | past perfect | *The train **had left** before we reached.* |
| tomorrow, next week, soon, in 2030 | will / going to | *The results **will be** out tomorrow.* |
| by (a future time), by the time | future perfect | *By 2030 they **will have built** the bridge.* |

blocks.title: Sequence of tenses
blocks.body:
When the main verb is in the **past**, the verb in the joined (subordinate) clause normally goes into a past form too:

- *He **said** that he **was** tired.* (not *is*)
- *I **thought** you **would** come.* (not *will*)
- *She **knew** that the bus **had left**.*

**Exceptions:** a universal truth or habitual fact stays in the present: *The teacher **said** that the earth **revolves** round the sun.*

A clause with *than* or *as* can take any tense the meaning needs: *She **liked** you more than she **likes** me.*

This rule is the heart of **reported speech** (Chapter 4), so master it here.

blocks.title: Solving a gap-filling passage, step by step
blocks.problem:
Fill in the blanks with the correct form of the verbs given in brackets:

Last Sunday our class (a) ____ (visit) the science museum. When we (b) ____ (reach), the guide (c) ____ (already, start) the tour, so we (d) ____ (join) the group quietly. Since then I (e) ____ (read) three books on space, and next year I (f) ____ (take) part in the science olympiad.
steps: (a) *Last Sunday* is a finished time → simple past: **visited**.
(b) A completed short action in the past story → simple past: **reached**.
(c) The tour started *before* we reached, and *already* confirms it → past perfect: **had already started**.
(d) The next action in the story → simple past: **joined**.
(e) *Since then* links the past to now → present perfect: **have read**.
(f) *next year* is the future → **will take** (or *am going to take*, a plan).
blocks.answer: visited, reached, had already started, joined, have read, will take

blocks.title: Editing: find the error, write the correction
blocks.problem:
Each line has one error. Write the incorrect word and the correction.

1. Yesterday I have met my old teacher in the market.
2. She did not knew that the shop was closed.
3. The earth moved round the sun, our teacher explained.
4. I am knowing him since my childhood.
steps: Line 1: *Yesterday* is a finished time; the present perfect cannot be used. **have met → met**.
Line 2: After *did* we always use V1. **knew → know**.
Line 3: A universal truth stays in the simple present. **moved → moves**.
Line 4: *know* is a stative verb, and *since my childhood* needs the present perfect. **am knowing → have known**.
blocks.answer: have met → met; knew → know; moved → moves; am knowing → have known

blocks.question: Find the error: *The guests have arrived an hour ago.*
blocks.explanation: *ago* marks a finished past time, so the simple past is needed: *The guests arrived an hour ago.*
option_feedback: *an hour ago* is correct; the verb is the problem.
Correct!
*have arrive* is not a correct form; and the real problem is *ago*.
*an hour* is correct, because *hour* begins with a vowel sound.

blocks.title: Three keys to every tense
blocks.body:
- **Be + ing = going on** (am/is/are/was/were/will be + V-ing).
- **Have + V3 = done** (has/have/had/will have + V3).
- **Have been + ing = going on for a while** (since / for).

**Did, does, do → always V1 after them.** "Did went" is a crime!

**Two past actions?** The one that happened **first** gets **had**.

**After when, if, as soon as → no *will*.**

blocks.title: The ten traps examiners love
blocks.body:
1. Present perfect with a past time: ✗ *I have seen it yesterday.* ✓ *I saw it yesterday.*
2. V2 after *did*: ✗ *He did not came.* ✓ *He did not come.*
3. Missing -s: ✗ *She go to school.* ✓ *She goes to school.*
4. Stative verbs in the continuous: ✗ *I am understanding.* ✓ *I understand.*
5. *Since* with a length of time: ✗ *since two years* ✓ *for two years*
6. *Will* in a time clause: ✗ *when he will come* ✓ *when he comes*
7. Wrong sequence: ✗ *He said that he is ill.* ✓ *He said that he was ill.*
8. Changing a universal truth: ✗ *She said the sun rose in the east.* ✓ *... rises in the east.*
9. Wrong V3: ✗ *has wrote, had went, have drank* ✓ *has written, had gone, have drunk*
10. Simple present for an action going on now: ✗ *Look! It rains.* ✓ *Look! It is raining.*

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Make a "tense ladder" on the board: one sentence, *Ravi eats lunch*, changed into all twelve tenses by the class, one student per step. Then play **Signal-word cricket**: the teacher calls out a signal word (*since, yesterday, Look!, by next year*), and each team must make a correct sentence in the right tense to score a run.

blocks.title: Say it in your own words
blocks.body: Explain to a friend the difference between *I have lived in Ahmedabad for ten years* and *I lived in Ahmedabad for ten years*. Who still lives there?

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Chapter 4, Reported Speech:** the sequence of tenses is used in every reported sentence.
- **Chapter 6–7, Editing and Gap Filling:** most board errors are tense errors.
- **Writing (letters and analytical paragraphs):** a data paragraph uses the past and present perfect; a letter of complaint uses the present perfect for problems still going on.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
Fill in the blanks with the correct form of the verbs in brackets:

The bell (a) ____ (ring) just now, but the teacher (b) ____ (not come) yet. The students (c) ____ (talk) loudly. Rohan (d) ____ (sit) quietly in the corner because he (e) ____ (forget) his homework at home. He hopes the teacher (f) ____ (not check) it today.

**Answer:** (a) **rang** (*just now* = a moment in the past) (b) **has not come** (*yet* → present perfect) (c) **are talking** (going on now) (d) **is sitting** (e) **has forgotten** / **forgot** (f) **will not check**.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- 3 times × 4 aspects = 12 tenses; learn their helping verbs from the map.
- Simple = fact/habit; continuous = going on; perfect = completed; perfect continuous = continuing for a period.
- Present perfect links the past to now; never use it with a finished past time.
- Past perfect marks the earlier of two past actions.
- In time and *if* clauses, use the present for the future.
- After a past reporting verb, shift the tense back, except for universal truths.
- *do/does/did* are always followed by V1.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- Read the **whole** sentence or passage before filling a blank; the signal word may come later.
- In editing, check the verb first: tense, -s agreement, and V1 after *did*.
- Write only the required answer in the format asked (for editing: *incorrect word → correction*).
- Spelling counts: *occurred, stopped, written, began, lying*.

blocks.front: Formula of the present perfect continuous?
blocks.back: has/have + been + V-ing: *She has been working since morning.*

blocks.front: Which tense for the earlier of two past actions?
blocks.back: Past perfect (had + V3): *The film had started before we arrived.*
since 2020 (point of time), for five years (length of time).

blocks.front: Correct: *If it will rain, we will stay home*?
blocks.back: *If it rains, we will stay home.* No *will* in an *if* or time clause.
